title: An Elegy upon the Death of Doctor Donne
short: Carew's elegy for Donne (d. 31 March 1631), printed among the 'Elegies upon the Author' in Donne's Poems (1633), is also a major early critique of his poetry.
body: John Donne, poet and from 1621 Dean of St Paul's, died on 31 March 1631. Thomas Carew (1595-1640), courtier and poet, wrote this elegy, which was printed with other tributes in the first edition of Donne's Poems (1633) and again in Carew's own Poems (1640). Poetry is 'widowed' because Donne, her husband, is dead; the opening question complains that no adequate elegy has yet appeared. The poem is one of the first critical assessments of Donne's 'wit' and his reform of English verse, and is frequently quoted in histories of the 'metaphysical' style.

title: unkneaded dough-baked prose
short: Half-baked, heavy prose, made from dough that was never kneaded: a jibe at the dull funeral sermons laid on Donne's dust.
body: 'Dough-baked' meant imperfectly baked, still doughy, and figuratively dull or half-witted (OED, dough-baked, a.). 'Unkneaded' adds that the material was never worked into shape. Carew asks why the poets have not trusted Donne's dust even to such inferior offerings as the prose of funeral sermons, implying that poets have been even more silent than preachers. The homely baking image, typical of Donne's own mixed diction, is set against the elevated elegiac occasion.

title: the unscissored lecturer
short: An 'unscissor'd' (unshorn, untrimmed) lecturer, a preacher whose withered rhetoric is as short-lived as his hour: a sneer at a dull preacher.
body: RPO glosses 'unscissor'd' as having uncut hair. A 'lecturer' was a preacher, often funded by a parish or town to give sermons in addition to the incumbent's services; such lectureships were frequently held by Puritans. Readers therefore sometimes take the jibe as aimed at a Puritan type, though the word itself proves only untidiness. The 'flower / Of fading Rhet'rique' is the flowery but perishable ornament of his style. The archive spelling 'uncizard' preserves an early form.

title: the pulpit hourglass
short: Pulpits had hourglasses timing the sermon; the lecturer's rhetoric is as dry as the sand running through it.
body: Early modern pulpits often had an hourglass fixed to them so that preacher and congregation could see the sermon's length, normally an hour (hence 'short-liv'd as his houre'). RPO identifies the sand as the hourglass's. The simile neatly unites dryness of style with the passing of time, and contrasts the measured, mechanical sermon with Donne's 'flame'. The image also hints at mortality, appropriate to a funeral sermon.

title: what the Pulpit retains
short: The pulpit may keep its plain precepts and doctrines; but the 'flame' of Donne's soul that set them alight 'must be desir'd for ever'.
body: The sentence is long and the archive lacks a comma after 'truth'. 'Her plaine, / And sober Christian precepts' are the plain moral teaching that the pulpit can keep without Donne. Carew's point is that doctrine, 'wholsome uses', homilies and lectures remain available to any preacher, whereas the 'flame' of Donne's soul, which moved the hearer's will through the eye and heart, has died with him. The passage is often quoted in discussions of how Donne's preaching and his poetry belong together.

title: doctrines and uses
short: Technical sermon terms: a Protestant sermon derived a 'doctrine' from the text and then applied it in 'uses' (practical applications).
body: William Perkins's influential manual of preaching (Latin 1592, English 1607) taught preachers to open the biblical text, collect doctrines from it, and apply them in 'uses', practical applications to the hearers' lives; the method became standard, especially among Puritans (OED, use, n., sense of application of doctrine in a sermon). 'Homilies' recalls the official Books of Homilies, and 'Lectures' were sermons outside the regular service (RPO). Carew lists the routine products of the pulpit to set off the power of Donne's preaching.

title: the flame of Donne's soul
short: Donne's soul shot out heat and light that burned the earth and lit its darkness; 'brighs' in the archive is a misprint for 'bright'.
body: Heat and light are traditional figures of zeal and illumination, and Pentecostal fire (Acts 2:3) of inspired preaching. 'Brave' means splendid, excellent. The archive's 'brighs' should read 'bright' (as in the Vincent text), restoring the rhyme with 'light'. Walton, who heard Donne preach, describes his sermons in similar terms of ardour, weeping and persuasion. The fire imagery runs throughout the elegy, through 'Promethean breath' to the burning laurel at the end.

anchor: Committed holy rapes upon the will
title: holy rapes upon the will
short: Donne's preaching seized and overpowered the will, the paradoxical violent conversion that he himself asked of God in 'Batter my heart'.
body: 'Rape' kept its Latin sense of seizure and carrying off (rapere), as in 'rapture', but the sexual sense was also present. The bold oxymoron echoes Donne's Holy Sonnet 'Batter my heart', which ends by asking God to 'ravish' him, since only so can he be chaste. Carew implies that Donne's sermons did to their hearers what Donne prayed God would do to him. The following line, 'through the eye the melting heart distill', uses alchemical language: the heart is melted and drawn off in tears.

anchor: the deepe knowledge, of darke truths
title: dark truths and fancy
short: Donne taught obscure truths so that sense could grasp what imagination could not reach: an account of his power to make the abstract concrete.
body: 'Sence' here means the bodily senses or plain understanding, and 'fancy' the imagination. Carew's claim is that Donne made difficult mysteries apprehensible, the reverse of what one might expect: he did not merely imagine beyond sense, but made the senses judge where even imagination failed. Later critics such as T. S. Eliot made a similar point about Donne's unified sensibility, his ability to feel thought. 'Must be desir'd for ever' (l. 21) closes the long sentence: this power is lost for good.

title: Delphic choir; Promethean breath
short: The 'Delphic quire' is the company of poets, servants of Apollo of Delphi; Donne's 'Promethean breath' first kindled their fire.
body: Delphi was Apollo's chief oracle, and Apollo was god of poetry; the Delphic 'quire' (choir) is therefore the poets. Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity (Hesiod, Theogony and Works and Days), and in some versions also shaped humans from clay. Donne is thus a culture-hero who brought new fire to English poetry; now that fire 'lyes quencht' in his death. The claim that Donne originated a poetic school is one of the elegy's influential judgements.

title: the Muses' garden
short: The standard texts read 'The Muses garden'; 'Moses' in the archive is a transcription error. Donne weeded pedantic imitation and planted fresh invention.
body: The 1633 text and modern editions read 'Muses' garden', the garden of poetry; 'Moses' here is a mistake in the archive's source. Donne 'purg'd' it of 'Pedantique weedes' (learned but lifeless borrowings) and 'the lazie seeds / Of servile imitation', replacing them with 'fresh invention' (in rhetoric, the finding of matter and argument). Carew's attack on 'servile imitation' is pointed, since Renaissance poetics, including Jonson's, prized the imitation of classical models. Here originality becomes the highest praise.

title: the bankrupt age
short: Donne paid the debts of a poor, bankrupt literary age that lived on borrowed classical wealth.
body: 'Banquerout' is an early form of 'bankrupt', from Italian banca rotta, the broken bench of a failed money-changer (OED, bankrupt). The financial metaphor runs through the passage: the age lives by 'thefts', Donne opens 'a Mine' of riches (l. 37), his gold is set against others' lead (l. 42), and he could have been the ancients' 'Exchequer' (l. 43). The economics of borrowing and originality is the elegy's central critical argument.

title: Anacreon and Pindar
short: Poets who fake inspiration by copying Anacreon's or Pindar's ecstasy produce a 'mimique furie'; 'Anacrcons' is a misprint for 'Anacreons'.
body: Anacreon (6th century BC) wrote light lyrics of wine and love, much imitated in the Renaissance from the pseudo-Anacreontic Anacreontea; Pindar (5th century BC) wrote lofty odes for athletic victors. RPO notes that both were considered great masters of the Greek ode. 'Poetique rage' is the Platonic furor poeticus, the divine madness of inspiration; Carew argues that imitators merely mimic it, being possessed by a borrowed ecstasy 'not their owne'. The archive spelling 'Anacrcons' is a typographical error.

title: sly exchanges and two-edged words
short: The trick of borrowing Greek and Latin words or double-meaning words; 'flie exchanges' should read 'slie' (sly) exchanges.
body: RPO glosses the wrong done to Greek and Latin (l. 36) as 'by borrowing Greek and Latin words'. The 'subtle cheate / Of slie exchanges' (the archive's 'flie' is a misreading of the long s in 'slie') suggests passing off foreign words as English, while 'jugling seate' (juggling feat, a conjuring trick) and 'two-edg'd words' point to ambiguous coinages that cut both ways. 'Whatsoever wrong / By ours was done the Greeke or Latine tongue' sums up this as plunder of the classics, which Donne has 'redeem'd' (in the financial sense of buying back a pledge).

title: masculine expression
short: Donne opened a 'mine' of pregnant fancy and drew a line of 'masculine' (strong, vigorous, rough) expression.
body: 'Masculine' in seventeenth-century criticism described a vigorous, compressed, argumentative style opposed to smooth, 'soft' or 'effeminate' sweetness (compare 'soft melting phrases', l. 53). The term belongs to the vocabulary of 'strong lines' in which Donne's admirers praised him. Modern critics have examined the gendered assumptions behind it. 'Pregnant fancie' (fertile imagination) mixes the metaphor oddly but tellingly with 'Masculine', and 'drawne a line' plays on a line of verse, a line of descent and a line drawn as a standard.

title: Orpheus and the ancient brood
short: Had Orpheus, the mythical first poet, or the other ancients seen Donne's work, they would have found him richer than themselves.
body: Orpheus, the legendary Thracian singer whose music moved stones and trees and who descended to the underworld for Eurydice, was the archetype of the poet (RPO). 'All the ancient brood / Our superstitious fooles admire' are the classical poets venerated by slavish modern imitators, who 'hold / Their Leade more precious then thy burnisht gold'. Carew here inverts the usual Renaissance hierarchy, ranking the modern Donne above the ancients: a bold move in the quarrel of ancients and moderns.

title: Exchequer; ore in dung
short: Donne would have been the ancients' treasury, and they would not have needed to search each other's dung for ore.
body: The Exchequer was the royal treasury and revenue court of England. The second line alludes to the story, preserved in the Suetonius-Donatus Life of Virgil, that when asked why he was reading Ennius, Virgil said he was gathering gold from Ennius' dung: i.e. salvaging fine things from a rough predecessor. Carew turns the anecdote into a jibe: the ancient poets borrowed from each other's leavings, whereas Donne mined his own gold.

title: the fate of language
short: Donne yields only to the ancients' priority in time and to the accident that Greek and Latin sound sweeter to the ear than English.
body: The ancients precede him only in time, and in the 'blind fate' that gave them languages whose 'tun'd chime' (musical sound, perhaps quantitative metre) charms the 'outward sense' (the ear) more than English. Carew argues that overcoming such a disadvantage earns Donne greater fame. The passage is an early example of the self-conscious comparison of English with the classical languages that runs from the sixteenth-century defences of the vernacular to Dryden.

title: the hooped language and giant fancy
short: English, 'troublesome' and tough, bends to Donne's 'imperious wit' and, like barrel hoops, binds a gigantic imagination too strong for softer tongues.
body: The image is of a cooper's barrel: the language's 'tough thick-rib'd hoopes' gird or bind Donne's 'Gyant fancie' (huge imagination), which would have burst the 'soft melting phrases' of Greek and Latin. 'Imperious' (commanding, masterful) keeps up the elegy's language of rule that culminates in the epitaph's 'King'. The lines themselves enact Donne's style, with knotted, consonantal monosyllables and strong enjambment.

title: rifled fields and gleaning
short: The ancients picked the prime buds of invention and left the fields stripped; yet from these bare lands Donne's mere gleanings exceed their whole harvest.
body: 'Cull the prime / Buds' means select the best blossoms; 'rifled fields' are plundered ones. Gleaning was the right of the poor to gather what the reapers left (Ruth 2; Leviticus 19:9-10). Carew's paradox is that Donne, coming late to exhausted ground, found more with his 'onely hands' (his hands alone, 'and that their smallest worke') than all earlier ages and languages reaped. The phrase 'besides the seate / To touch their harvest' is difficult; the sense seems to be that the ancients left the fields stripped, with only the bare ground remaining.

anchor: Too hard for Libertines in Poetrie
title: libertines in poetry
short: Without Donne's 'strict laws', poetic 'libertines', poets who refuse discipline, will return to old licences.
body: A 'libertine' was a freethinker in religion or a dissolute person; here, a poet who takes liberties with form and matter. The phrase carries irony, since Carew himself was known for libertine love poetry such as 'A Rapture'. The 'strickt lawes' and 'just raigne' cast Donne as a lawgiver-king whose death will bring anarchy, preparing for the epitaph's 'Monarchie of wit'.

title: the exiled train of gods
short: Donne banished the classical gods and Ovidian tales from 'nobler poems'; after him the libertines will bring back the Metamorphoses. 'Ttaine' is a misprint for 'traine'.
body: Donne's poetry does indeed largely avoid the mythological machinery common in Elizabethan verse (Venus, Cupid, Ovidian narratives such as Marlowe's Hero and Leander). Carew imagines that machinery as a 'goodly' (handsome) 'traine' of exiled deities waiting to return. RPO notes that Ovid's Metamorphoses, with its lavish tales of gods and goddesses, strongly influenced sixteenth-century poetry. 'Silenc'd tales' and 'windie page' scorn such narrative as empty and inflated. The archive 'ttaine' is a typographical error for 'traine'.

title: ballad-rhyme and apostasy
short: Verse 'refin'd' by Donne will decline into ballad jingle or worship old idols with 'new Apostasie'; 'resin'd' is a misprint for 'refin'd'.
body: The archive's 'resin'd' misreads the long s of 'refin'd'. 'Ballad-rime' means the crude rhymes of popular broadside ballads, the lowest kind of verse in courtly eyes. 'Idols' and 'Apostasie' (abandonment of the true faith) apply religious language to literary history: the return of pagan gods in poetry is a relapse into idolatry, a joke made sharper by Donne's having become a priest. 'This last Age' may suggest the last age of the world, as well as the most recent.

title: the spinning wheel
short: A wheel keeps turning a little after the hand leaves it, by its 'first impulsive force'; so the poet's feeble verse continues from Donne's impulse.
body: The standard text reads 'swiftly-turning wheel' (the archive's 'tuning' omits a letter, and 'saint' in l. 81 is a misprint for 'faint'). The image may be a potter's or spinning wheel. 'Impulsive' means impelling, driving forward (RPO); the idea of a moving body retaining an impressed force derives from the scholastic theory of impetus. Carew's modesty topos makes his own elegy a dying motion of Donne's art: the arts' 'influence', grown feeble, 'gasps' in his 'panting numbers' (metres).

title: the reverend silence
short: Carew apologises for breaking the silence around the hearse, a silence that was itself a louder elegy, a 'dumbe Eloquence'.
body: The apology is a conventional elegiac humility formula, but the paradox of a silence more eloquent than verse ('a loude Elegie', 'dumbe Eloquence') is in Donne's own manner. The 'death of all the Arts' expresses the extravagant claim that Donne's death leaves eloquence itself expiring; 'panting numbers' and 'Gasping short-winded accents' imitate the dying breath in irregular rhythm. Compare the opening question about whether poetry can produce 'one Elegie'.

title: the crackling bay crown
short: The poet's laurel thrown on Donne's funeral pyre crackles and 'spits disdain' before turning to ash; 'stile' should read 'pile'.
body: Bay (laurel) was sacred to Apollo and the crown of poets. In Roman practice laurel was burned in rituals, and its crackling in the flame was read as an omen (Tibullus 2.5.81-84; compare the laurel in Virgil's Eclogue 8.82-83). Carew imagines the crown on the pyre crackling as if it disdains the fire, i.e. the poetic fame of Donne resists destruction until the flames consume its moisture. The archive's 'funerall stile' is apparently an error for 'funerall pile' (pyre); the ancient image of cremation is a literary fiction, since Donne was buried in St Paul's.

title: engross
short: He will not incur envy by trying to 'engross' (write out in full, or monopolise) all Donne's perfections.
body: RPO glosses 'engross' as to draw up a complete list, the legal sense of writing a document out in large fair hand (OED, engross, v.). The word also meant to monopolise, to buy up the whole supply, which fits 'draw the envy': he will not seize all the praise for himself. 'Let others carve the rest' anticipates the epitaph by imagining tributes cut in stone; 'incize' (l. 92) means cut or engrave.

title: the universal monarchy of wit
short: The epitaph crowns Donne absolute king of wit, ruling 'as he thought fit': one of the most quoted phrases in Donne criticism.
body: 'Universal monarchy' was a political term for the world empire attributed to the ambitions of Spain and the Habsburgs; Carew applies it to Donne's absolute dominion over wit (intelligence, invention, ingenious conceit). 'Rul'd as he thought fit' suggests the absolutist language of Stuart kingship as well as Donne's freedom from rules. The couplet has fixed Donne's reputation as the founder and sovereign of a school of 'wit', a view later developed by Dryden and Samuel Johnson in his account of the 'metaphysical poets'.

title: two Flamens
short: A flamen was a Roman priest of a single god; Donne was two priests in one, first Apollo's (poetry), at last the 'true God's'.
body: The flamines were Roman priests each dedicated to one deity, such as the Flamen Dialis of Jupiter (RPO notes that flamens were Roman priests). Carew's conclusion divides Donne's career into the secular poet ('Apollo's first') and the ordained divine (he took orders in 1615 and became Dean of St Paul's in 1621). RPO reads the line as alluding to the move from secular to religious poetry. The neat division, echoed by Walton's Life, has been both influential and disputed, since Donne's 'two' vocations overlapped.

title: couplets and enjambment
short: Heroic couplets with heavy enjambment and long periodic sentences, imitating Donne's 'strong-lined' manner while praising it.
body: The elegy is in iambic pentameter couplets, but the sense runs on across couplets and lines (e.g. ll. 11-21, one sentence), with caesuras in unexpected places, unlike the end-stopped couplets later perfected by Waller and Dryden. This 'masculine' roughness enacts the style the poem describes. Carew, often counted among the 'Cavalier' poets and influenced by Jonson, here shows his debt to Donne. Critics often read the elegy as a pivotal text between Donne's generation and the Restoration's critical vocabulary.
